title: The intelligence layer for adaptive systems
subtitle: TheAdaply turns real work, from engineering sessions to robot trajectories, into tested improvements the whole team can reuse.
description: The TheAdaply thesis: capture real work, test proposed improvements against the current setup, and reuse what passes. Software engineering agents today; robotics on the same learning loop.

sections.heading: The thesis
paragraphs: Every task your team completes should make its agents better at the next one. TheAdaply’s thesis is to turn the lessons in everyday work, from successful approaches to review feedback, into improvements the whole team can reuse.

We start with software engineering agents. TheAdaply is for engineering teams that want their AI agents to produce better work than the team achieves today, with less direction, review and correction. We start with the team’s goals, accepted work and feedback, then test changes to agents’ instructions, tools and approaches against its own criteria. The search includes approaches the team has not yet tried.

We compare each change with the current setup on the same tasks, then test the strongest on fresh tasks. We measure the quality of the work and the time people spend guiding agents, reviewing results and correcting the same mistakes. Improvements that pass become the starting point for the next round.

Suppose an engineer’s agent works out how to move a service to a new system on Monday. TheAdaply tests the approach and saves the checks that made it work. On Tuesday, a teammate’s agent can use the accepted pattern where it applies and verify its own work. Sharing follows the team’s permissions.

The same problem exists beyond software. A robot’s work also leaves a trajectory: what it observed, what it was asked to do, what it tried, where it failed, where a person stepped in, and whether the outcome was accepted. Today most of that experience is thrown away. TheAdaply extends the same loop to robotics: capture the trajectory, keep what is useful, test a proposed adaptation against the current baseline, and retain it only when it passes.

sections.heading: Customer case: completing a UI brief
paragraphs: One customer wanted a design system that accounted for the different states a product can reach. They asked whether a skill could help an agent complete the UI details they left open. They described the current process this way:

sections.heading: Make the remaining UI decisions visible
paragraphs: Consider a possible next request: “Add a team members page with invitations.” A table and invite button leave much unresolved: loading, failed invitations, permissions and narrow screens. Each missing state can send the customer back into another round of decisions and corrections.

The proposed workflow starts from the customer’s accepted patterns and review corrections. The agent inspects existing components and design documentation, then maps relevant states and checks before implementation. It cites conventions for supported details and puts unsupported choices in front of the customer.

Product decisions stay with the customer when no authoritative rule settles them. “Can a member invite people, or only an admin?” is a question to resolve before code. The table shows some of the decisions and checks this brings forward.

sections.heading: Test for better results and less review
paragraphs: Once the customer resolves those choices, the agent implements the page with existing components, runs focused tests and checks the result in the browser. A review agent checks the agreed states and design patterns. The customer can review the flow against explicit decisions and checks.

To decide whether to adopt this workflow, we compare it with the current setup and a generic improvement on the same UI tasks, then test it on fresh tasks. The comparison covers missed states, correctness and consistency with accepted patterns, alongside review effort, time and cost. Retain the change only if the work improves against the customer’s criteria with less human effort.

The same discipline holds outside software, with acceptance criteria that fit the domain. Software evaluation weighs correctness, test results, regressions, review effort, time and cost. Robotics evaluation weighs task success, recovery, intervention rate, completion time and safety constraints where they are measured. We do not reuse one domain’s criteria for the other.

caseNote: This is the kind of work TheAdaply can learn from: the customer’s specifications, accepted designs and review corrections. The proposed improvement is a workflow for turning a partial UI brief into a page the customer can review with fewer omissions.

explorerTitle: Inspect the setup for this customer case
explorerDescription: The bundle shows how the preparation and review in this example become part of the agent’s setup. A skill sets out the procedure; instructions make it the default for UI tasks. A review agent checks the agreed states, and a hook provides a reminder. The model and its permissions stay the same. This bundle is a concrete example of adapting a software-agent setup; other improvements, and robotic adaptations especially, use different components under the same evaluation discipline.
closing: Each accepted improvement should give the team’s next agent a stronger starting point.

specPreview.title: A reviewable specification before implementation
specPreview.description: For the same team members page, separate decisions the customer needs to make from details the agent can support with existing conventions.

rows.decision: Can a member invite people, or only an admin?
rows.behavior: Ask the customer unless an authoritative rule settles it.
rows.checks: Test allowed and denied roles once resolved.

rows.behavior: Reuse that component; show the invite action only to an allowed role.
rows.checks: Render an empty result for each relevant role.

rows.decision: What should a duplicate invitation do?
rows.behavior: Propose keeping the email input and reusing the form-error pattern, if established.
rows.checks: Exercise request failure and the agreed duplicate behavior.

rows.decision: Which responsive and dialog conventions apply?
rows.behavior: Reuse established conventions; propose visible focus, focus return and no horizontal overflow.
rows.checks: Review a narrow viewport and complete the flow by keyboard.

conclusion: Our longer-term direction is to adapt private models using work that passes the team’s checks. Further out, the same direction applies to robot policies adapted from evaluated trajectories; that is a direction, not something implemented today. We will compare adapted models with the team’s existing options on quality, cost and control over data before adopting them.
